summary: Defines the textual conventions and the general group of MIB objects for IPv6. It is the base of a series of IPv6 MIB documents. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 4293 and RFC 8096.

eli5.summary: These are the first dials in a set for watching IPv6 behavior in a network. Newer documents replaced them.

subtitle: The foundation for watching and managing IPv6 networks

tldr.problem: IPv6 is a new version of the Internet Protocol with 128-bit addresses that cannot fit into existing management information formats. Network managers need standard tools to monitor IPv6 networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines textual conventions that represent IPv6 data types in SNMP, and creates six tables that track IPv6 interfaces, their statistics, address prefixes, assigned addresses, routing information, and address-to-physical-address mappings.
tldr.outcome: This document provides the foundation for all IPv6 management, serving as the base that other IPv6 MIB modules build upon, though it is now historic and replaced by RFC 4293 and RFC 8096.

today: RFC 2465 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 4293 and RFC 8096, which provide updated MIB definitions for IPv6 management using modern SNMP and data modeling standards.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Representation in Management
sections.content:
Management Information Bases (MIBs) describe what can be watched on a network. However, the original MIB data types were designed for IPv4 addresses, which are 32 bits. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits: four times larger.

This RFC solves the problem by defining new textual conventions, ways of encoding IPv6 data, that fit within SNMP's existing framework. An IPv6 address is represented as a 16 octet binary string (128 bits total) in network byte order. The RFC also defines conventions for IPv6 address prefixes (up to 16 octets), interface identifiers (up to 8 octets), and interface indexes.
sections.eli5: The old format could only write down short addresses. This book says how to write down long addresses using the language the manager already speaks.

sections.title: The Six Tables of the IPv6 General Group
sections.content:
The RFC defines six tables that form the foundation of IPv6 management:

The Interface Table (ipv6IfTable) describes each IPv6 interface on a device, including its description, the protocol layer below it, its maximum transmission unit (MTU), its address identifier, and its administrative and operational status.

The Interface Statistics Table (ipv6IfStatsTable) records counters for each interface: packets received, packets with header errors, packets that could not be forwarded, packets successfully delivered, fragments that needed reassembly, multicast packets, and more.

The Address Prefix Table (ipv6AddrPrefixTable) lists the IPv6 address prefixes, the network portions of addresses, associated with each interface, including the prefix length and lifetime information.

The Address Table (ipv6AddrTable) records which complete IPv6 addresses are assigned to each interface, when they were created, and whether they are being used.

The Route Table (ipv6RouteTable) describes the routes that the device uses to forward IPv6 packets to their destinations.

The Address Translation Table (ipv6NetToMediaTable) maps IPv6 addresses to physical (link-layer) addresses, similar to an ARP table for IPv6.
sections.eli5: The book explains six notebooks: one for interfaces, one for counting packets on each interface, one for address blocks, one for individual addresses, one for routes, and one for finding physical addresses.

sections.title: Managing IPv6 Devices
sections.content:
Several objects in the IPv6 MIB can be read and changed by network managers. The ipv6Forwarding object indicates whether a device is acting as a router (forwarding packets not addressed to itself) or as a host. Managers can change this setting to turn routing on or off.

The ipv6DefaultHopLimit object sets the default hop limit (similar to TTL in IPv4) for packets the device sends. This controls how far a packet can travel before being discarded.

Interface administrative status can be changed to bring interfaces up or down. Interface descriptions can be updated to reflect changes in network topology.
sections.eli5: The manager can flip some switches: turn routing on or off, set how far packets can travel, and bring interfaces up or down.

sections.title: Key IPv6 Concepts in the MIB
sections.content:
The RFC introduces several IPv6-specific concepts:

Link-local addresses are unique only on a single link. Each IPv6 interface automatically gets a link-local address. An interface index is needed to distinguish between the same link-local address on different interfaces.

Address prefixes define which portion of an address is the network and which is the device. A prefix length of 64 means the first 64 bits are the network.

Interface identifiers are the device-specific part of an address that gets combined with a prefix to form a complete address. Many interfaces autoconfigure these identifiers from their physical (MAC) addresses.

Duplicate Address Detection is an IPv6 mechanism that ensures each address on a link is unique. If detection fails, an interface cannot move to operational status and gets the noIfIdentifier state.

Fragmentation and reassembly counters show whether packets are being broken into smaller pieces and reassembled, which impacts performance.
sections.eli5: Some addresses only work on one cable. Addresses are made of two parts: a network part and a device part. Devices check that addresses are not used twice. When packets are too big, they get split up and taped back together.

sections.title: Security of IPv6 Management
sections.content:
The IPv6 MIB exposes significant information about network topology and operation. Knowing which interfaces exist, what addresses are used, and what routes are configured helps an attacker understand the network structure.

Additionally, the ability to change forwarding status, hop limits, and interface status is powerful: an attacker could disable critical interfaces or turn a host into a router.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with user-based authentication and view-based access control to restrict who can read the MIB and who can make changes. Strong encryption is important because IPv6 data could be intercepted in transit.
sections.eli5: Knowing how a network is wired helps attackers find weak spots. You need a strong lock so only trusted people can look at the plans or change them.
